title: How to answer repeated roadmap questions from executives on Mac: a PM routine for 2026
metaTitle: Answer repeated roadmap questions from executives on Mac
description: Stop answering the same roadmap questions by hand. Use one shared link, a standard reply and a weekly routine that works on a Mac.
targetKeyword: answer repeated roadmap questions from executives
intro: To answer repeated roadmap questions from executives, give them one current link and one standard written answer. Then send every new question back to that answer instead of rebuilding it from memory. This page covers what the repeats cost, why they keep coming back, and fixes you can use on a Mac without buying anything.
tldr: Put one current roadmap link at the top of every executive update. The same question then gets one answer.
Write a two-line standard answer for each question you hear often. Keep it in a snippet or a Notion page.
Post the update on a fixed day, so executives know when new information arrives.
Lazur can draft and dictate the reply. You check the facts and send it yourself.

blocks.text: Your week has a familiar shape. A director asks where the search rework landed. A little later, a VP asks the same thing in a different channel. You answer both from memory, and the answers do not quite match. The question is not hard. It keeps coming back because the answer lives in your head and in old threads, not in one place people can find.
What repeated roadmap questions cost you

No survey I found measures how often product managers get repeat roadmap questions. The figures below are general knowledge-worker numbers. They point the same way, but they do not prove your week looks like someone else's.

Start with money, because it is the easiest to picture. The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a median base pay of $49.19 an hour for project management specialists in May 2025. A product manager is a different job, so treat the figure as a rough stand-in. Base pay also leaves out benefits and overhead, so your real cost is higher.
Turn the cost into a number you can defend

Use one simple formula. Add up the minutes each repeat answer takes, including the time to find the context. Multiply by the repeats in a week. Then multiply by your hourly base pay. Count for one full week before you estimate. A guess made at the start is easy for a skeptical manager to dismiss.

items: Search Slack and your doc tool for roadmap, timeline, launch and status. Cover the last two weeks.
Count each message or meeting question where you explained the plan again.
Time one typical repeat answer, from reading the question to sending the reply.
Multiply the total minutes by your hourly base pay. Save the figure and compare it next month.

blocks.text: Why executives keep asking the same roadmap questions

Executives are usually not ignoring the roadmap. They cannot find the current version quickly. They also do not trust that a copy they saw last month is still true. Atlassian reports that 56% of employees still ping someone or schedule a meeting to get the information they need. Asking is often the fastest path to an answer.

Distance adds to the problem. Berkeley Haas summarized a Microsoft study of over 61,000 employees. Workers collaborated less across groups, and written channels replaced live talk. A written update reaches people unevenly, so each leader sees a different slice of the plan.
Find the questions before you answer them

Most repeat questions follow a pattern. The same few themes come back, such as a date, a scope change or a dependency. Log them for one week, and the pattern shows up. Memory is not a reliable log, so use a sheet.

In Google Sheets, make four columns: date, who asked, the question in their words, and theme. Select the header row and choose Data > Create a filter. Then filter by theme to see which answers you repeat most. To count distinct themes quickly, read [how to count unique values in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/count-unique-values-in-google-sheets).

rows: The date moved, or the owner changed
Current date, the date you can defend, and what would move it
Is this still on the roadmap?
Scope changed in a meeting nobody summarized
Yes or no, the reason, and a link to the decision
Why is team B waiting on us?
The dependency is unclear to the person asking
The dependency, its owner and the date it clears

blocks.text: Watch for questions that look repeated but are not. A director who asks about a date after a scope change needs a new answer. Log the change as well as the question, so you can tell the two apart later.
Write one standard answer for each repeat question

Write each answer once, in the same format. Two lines work for most repeats. The first line gives the current status and date. The second line says what changed since the last update, then links to the source. Date every answer, so a reader can see when it was last true.

Store answers where your hands already are. That can be a Notion page, a pinned message in the channel or a snippet in your dictation setup. Lazur dictates clean text at the cursor in any app when you hold fn. It also keeps snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots.
Make one roadmap link the answer

The fastest fix is one link that always shows the current state. Productboard documents the steps for its own boards. Open Share > Publish, then Copy link. Anyone with the link can view the board unless you set a passcode. Only makers or admins can publish, and the board must sit in an open teamspace.

blocks.title: Check the copies
blocks.text: Unpublishing turns off links and embeds right away. It does not remove copies someone already pasted into a slide, doc or email. Search for those copies before you say the old link is gone.

Know what viewers see before you share. Productboard's help page says viewers see item names, descriptions, status values and card attributes. They cannot open other boards or the rest of the workspace. Treat anything on the card as visible to anyone with that link.
Decide what goes in the shared view

items: Include the status, the current target date, the owner and the last-changed date.
Include one line on what is committed and what is only a hypothesis.
Leave out salary, hiring plans, customer names and unreleased pricing unless your company says they are safe to share.
Leave out internal debate and half-finished options that will confuse the reader.

blocks.text: Set one update time, then keep it

A fixed time changes behavior. If executives know the roadmap note lands on the same day each week, they stop asking in the meantime. Pick a slot your team can keep, and post the note in the channel executives already read. Put the slot on your calendar, too.

Ask Lazur out loud to set a reminder or a Calendar event for the update. Lazur sets Apple Reminders and Calendar events by voice. Check the item once after you set it, so you know it saved. Keep the reminder short, so you do not skip it in a busy week.
When an executive asks anyway

Some people will still ask. Answer with the link and the one line that changed. Do not reopen the whole plan in the thread. If the question shows the roadmap is unclear, say so and offer a short review call. That costs both calendars less than another long thread.

Ask what decision they need to make. Many repeats come from someone who has a choice coming up and wants the date to lock in. A direct question often ends the loop faster than any document. Write down the answer, then add it to your standard replies.
Mistakes that make repeat questions worse

items: Sharing a draft as if it were final. Mark drafts clearly, or keep them out of the shared view.
Updating the link but not the copies in slides and docs. Old copies restart the cycle.
Answering only in direct messages, so the next person asks the same question again.
Putting dates in the roadmap that the team has not agreed to. The roadmap then reads as a promise.
Writing long updates nobody opens. Two lines and a link usually beat a full page.

blocks.text: Check whether the routine works

Count repeat questions for a month, using the same search terms and the same sheet each week. A drop is a useful signal, but it is not proof. I did not find a controlled study showing that a roadmap page or FAQ cuts repeat questions. Your own count is the best evidence you will get.

Also check quality. A quiet inbox can mean people stopped asking because they stopped trusting the roadmap. Ask two executives each month whether the update answered what they needed. Keep the parts they say help.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate text at the cursor in any app. Use it to draft the two-line answer, read back a dense status page, or point at the control you need.

Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It does not post to Slack, edit your roadmap or know what an executive means. You read every draft and send it yourself. It also cannot give a roadmap a clear owner. That still takes a person.
Sensitive details in a shared roadmap

Roadmaps often mention customers, pricing, hiring or unreleased features. Before you share a link outside your team, check your company's rules for that kind of detail. Some companies require an admin review. Follow your employer's rules on client or patient data, even when the roadmap feels internal.

faq.question: What does it mean to answer repeated roadmap questions from executives?
faq.answer: It means you stop rebuilding the same answer from memory each time. You give executives one current link, one dated written answer and one fixed update time. Then you point each new question back to those. The goal is fewer repeats and answers that match.

faq.question: Is there data on how often product managers get repeat roadmap questions?
faq.answer: Not that I found. The studies on this page measure knowledge workers in general. Atlassian says leaders and teams waste 25% of their time searching for answers. Use your own one-week count to test that against your team.

faq.question: Should I share the full roadmap through a public link?
faq.answer: Not by default. A link that anyone can open can reach people outside the team. Set a passcode if your tool offers one. Check what viewers can see before you send the link to anyone new.

faq.question: Does Lazur post the update to Slack for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can draft the update and dictate it at the cursor. It does not click send or operate Slack for you. You read the text and send it yourself.

faq.question: How do I know the routine is working?
faq.answer: Count the roadmap questions that reach you each week, using the same search terms and sheet. Compare the counts over a month. Also ask two executives whether each update answered their question. A low count can mislead, because people may have stopped trusting the roadmap.

faq.question: What if the roadmap changes every week?
faq.answer: Then the roadmap is the problem, not only the answers. Mark it as a working draft, show the date it was last checked and agree on what counts as a commitment. Each change still needs a one-line note, or the repeats return.

faq.question: Does this apply to regulated or client-facing work?
faq.answer: Roadmaps can include customer data, so follow your employer's rules on sharing that data. Do not paste client or patient details into an AI tool unless your company allows it. When in doubt, describe the item without the sensitive detail.

costs.title: Minutes that add up across a week
costs.text: Each repeat answer costs more than the minutes you spend typing it. You also lose the thread you were working on and have to rebuild it. The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a median base pay of $49.19 an hour for project management specialists in May 2025. A product manager is not the same job, so treat that as a rough stand-in. It is base pay only, not the full cost to your company.

costs.title: Work about work crowds out the real job
costs.text: Asana defines work about work as communicating about work, searching for information and chasing the status of work. It says 60% of a person's time at work goes to that kind of work, not to skilled work. Repeat roadmap questions fall into the same bucket. They take your time without moving the product forward.

costs.title: Trust and speed with leadership
costs.text: Atlassian reports that 74% of leaders say poor communication is directly hurting their team's speed and output. When executives keep asking, they may doubt the answer they already have. Every repeat slows the decision they are waiting on. It can also signal that the roadmap is hard to read.

costs.title: Decisions made on old information
costs.text: A repeat question often means the asker last saw an older version. They may plan a launch, a hire or a customer promise around a date that already moved. The cost shows up later, in rework and in apologies. It is hard to put a number on it, so count the cases you can see.

causes.title: The current answer is hard to find
causes.text: Atlassian reports that 56% of employees still ping someone or schedule a meeting to get the information they need. For a product manager, that means an executive would rather ask than search. If the latest version sits in a slide deck, a doc and a thread, asking is the faster path. The fix is to make the current answer the easiest one to find.

causes.title: Updates arrive in channels that scroll away
causes.text: Berkeley Haas summarized research on remote work at Microsoft. It found that workers shifted toward asynchronous channels such as email and messaging and away from live conversations. A written update posted on Monday gets buried by Thursday. The executive who missed it asks again, and nobody thinks that is strange.

causes.title: Teams stay siloed
causes.text: The same Microsoft study, published in Nature Human Behaviour in 2021, found that remote work made collaboration networks less interconnected and more siloed. Workers spent about 25% less time collaborating with colleagues across groups. An executive in one group may never see the update sent to another group. Your roadmap can be correct and still miss the people who ask.

causes.title: Coordination takes the time you need for strategy
causes.text: Pragmatic Institute's 2025 State of Product Management and Marketing report says much of the time reclaimed from routine work goes to coordination and alignment. It does not go to market learning or clearer decisions. The report gives no time split, so treat this as a pattern, not a measured share of your week.

causes.title: Nobody agreed on what the roadmap promises
causes.text: Gallup reports that 76% of employees strongly agree they know what is expected of them when they are included in goal setting. That figure drops to 47% when they are not. Executives who were not part of the goals often ask again because they do not know what was promised. The data is correlational, so it does not prove cause, but the pattern is hard to ignore.

fixes.title: Publish one live link and stop sending copies
fixes.text: Keep one view that always shows the current state, and send only that link. Productboard's help page shows the mechanism for its own boards, including who can publish and what viewers see. Measure your repeat count for a month after you switch, so you know whether the change helped your team.

fixes.title: Give every repeat question a written answer
fixes.text: Write a standard answer for each question that keeps coming back. Use the same format every time: status and date, what changed, and the link. Date each answer so a reader can see when it was last true. Refresh those dates on your weekly update day, not whenever you remember.

fixes.title: Agree on commitments with the people who ask
fixes.text: Gallup's goal-setting finding points to a simple step. Include the executives who depend on the roadmap in the goal conversation, and write down what the team committed to. Mark anything else as a hypothesis. Shared goals do not guarantee fewer questions. They do give you a clear reference when a question comes up.

fixes.title: Search before you answer
fixes.text: Check Slack and your doc tool before you reply. Notion's releases page describes its Find feature as giving answers with citations. That is the vendor's own description, so test it on your pages before you rely on it. A search that finds an old version is worse than no search, so check the date on every hit.

fixes.title: Keep internal notes out of the shared view
fixes.text: Notion's releases page describes column permissions added in Notion 3.7. Database owners can choose which properties each person or agent can view or edit. Use that kind of control to keep risk notes or budget columns out of a database you share. Confirm that your plan and workspace settings include the feature first.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Update the one link
plan.text: Open the single roadmap view you share. Check statuses, dates and owners. Edit the text around the link if the view changed. Keep one live link, not copies pasted into three places.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Log the questions
plan.text: Search the last two weeks of Slack threads and meeting notes for roadmap questions. Put each question in a sheet with a column for the answer you gave. Filter by theme to see the repeats.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Write the standard answers
plan.text: For each repeat question, write a two-line answer in the same format. Store it as a snippet or on a Notion page. Include the link and the date you last checked the facts.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Send the update
plan.text: Post the weekly note in the channel executives already read. Keep it short. Lead with what changed, then the link. Dictate with fn if writing the note takes too long.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Count and adjust
plan.text: Count how many roadmap questions reached you this week and compare the count with the week before. Keep the change that cut repeats. Drop anything that added noise without helping.
